Major European Education Powerhouses Record Historic Lows in Latest Global Pisa Study

31 Oct 2026, 11:15 AM IST · GlobeWire Daily Education Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

The release of the 2025 Pisa scores has revealed severe academic declines across several of western Europe's leading education systems, with France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Finland all posting historically low results. The triennial study, administered by the OECD, measures how effectively 15-year-olds apply their knowledge in reading, mathematics, and science to real-world scenarios.

While England bucked the broader regional trend, results across continental Europe extended a downward trajectory that began around 2018. In the hardest-hit nations, approximately one in three 15-year-olds now lacks basic functional literacy and mathematics skills.

Country-Specific Findings and Reactions

In Germany, pupils recorded their worst-ever Pisa performance. The findings indicate that roughly one in four students lacks basic competency in natural sciences, while one in three falls short in reading and mathematics. The study highlighted a stark socioeconomic divide within Europe's largest economy: only 2% of pupils from low-income families achieved high competence levels, compared with 25% from higher-income households. Samuel Greiff, the German Pisa study coordinator, emphasized that family background exerts a much stronger influence on academic success in Germany than in peer nations like Denmark or Norway. German Education Minister Karin Prien called for urgent measures by the end of the year, pointing to the negative impacts of excessive social media use.

In the Netherlands, reading literacy scores reached a historic low, with 39% of 15-year-olds lacking the foundational skills needed to evaluate sources or navigate multi-page texts—an increase from 33% in the 2022 assessment. Researchers noted that Dutch reading levels have fallen by more than 60 points over the past decade. While the Dutch education ministry acknowledged the results as a structural issue rather than a temporary post-pandemic dip, unions and advocacy groups pushed back. The AOb teachers' union argued that chronic class cancellations, reliance on unqualified staff, and heavy workloads are driving educators away.

France also registered its worst results on record. Education Minister Édouard Geffray acknowledged the concerning figures, while analysts pointed to long-standing issues including insufficient primary school investment, high educational inequality, and frequent leadership turnover, with eight education ministers over the past decade.

Even in Finland, historically regarded as a global educational leader, average scores declined in both reading and mathematics compared to 2022. Dr. Arto K. Ahonen, the Finnish Pisa national project manager, noted that the results have sparked internal discussions regarding student perseverance and the necessity of modernizing school curricula.

Underlying Causes and Broader Context

Education experts attribute the widespread declines to a combination of factors. Beyond pandemic-related disruptions, systems have struggled with chronic teacher shortages, widening inequalities within segregated school networks, and frequent curricular shifts that critics argue have neglected foundational skills. Furthermore, researchers noted that pervasive smartphone use and digital distraction have heavily eroded student attention spans and motivation, depressing rates of deep reading.

Practical Implications and What Readers Can Verify

Readers tracking international educational benchmarks can review the complete data set and country-specific reports directly through the official OECD Pisa portal.

  • What is confirmed: The 2025 Pisa report documents falling average scores in reading, mathematics, and science across France, Germany, the Netherlands, and Finland, with roughly one in three students lacking basic functional literacy and numeracy in the most affected nations. Officials and researchers across these countries have acknowledged structural challenges, including socioeconomic disparities and digital distractions.
  • What remains unknown: The precise timeline and long-term efficacy of individual national policy responses—such as Germany's planned youth protection measures or Dutch curricular overhauls—have yet to be determined.
  • How to verify: Original reporting and primary data points can be accessed via The Guardian's coverage at The Guardian, as well as through official OECD publications detailing the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment.
